<reason>PRO built a clean frame (money settles labor status; only the voice question remains) and landed a genuinely damaging line—that CON's counsel-negotiated consent decrees are bargaining "minus the ratification vote and minus the shield." But CON won more of the concrete clash. CON forced PRO to concede "partial unionization," then showed its costs: only the Big Ten qualifies, the SEC produces zero units, transfer/eligibility terms PRO itself listed would split into two rulebooks for one playoff, and the antitrust shield is a wash for the unshielded half. CON's sharpest point—wrestlers who receive no revenue share are not employees on PRO's own logic and therefore cannot sit in the unit—went unanswered in PRO's closing, undercutting PRO's "department-wide unit" rescue. CON also answered both pressure questions directly (risk-on-one-path vs certainty-on-the-other; consent decrees with continuing jurisdiction) and correctly called out PRO's "institution alone" strawman. CON's two clipped turns are a real execution cost, and PRO's consent/legitimacy argument stays live, which keeps this competitive rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B2.1]–[B2.3] flipping PRO's "the check settles employment" premise—payment is licensing, the union petition is what triggers the classification cascade—reframed the whole cost debate, and CON sustained it in [B4.1]–[B4.2] and [B4.7] by showing PRO's own logic excludes wrestlers from any bargaining unit.</best_rebuttal>
